Day 69 of 100 · Docker

Container Security

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityDockerPublished journey entry

Container security reduces what a compromised application can do by removing unnecessary identity, filesystem, capability and host privileges.

Architecture / mental model

image controls + runtime controls → least-privileged container → limited host impact

How it works

The application should run as a non-root identity when it does not require root. A Dockerfile can create an application account and switch to it with `USER`, then runtime identity can be checked with `id`.

A read-only root filesystem prevents writes to most of the container filesystem. If the application needs writable state, provide only the required path with a volume or tmpfs instead of making the entire root filesystem writable.

Linux capabilities should be dropped aggressively and added back only when the workload needs a specific capability. `--privileged` removes too many isolation controls to be a casual compatibility switch.

Hands-on reference

docker run --rm myapp:1.0 id
docker run --read-only myapp:1.0
docker run --cap-drop=ALL myapp:1.0

Verification

Check the runtime UID/GID, attempt an unnecessary write to the root filesystem, inspect capabilities and run the application's legitimate workload to ensure the reduced privileges still meet requirements.

Field note / gotcha

When a security control breaks a legitimate write, the answer is usually a scoped writable mount or tmpfs, not restoring write access to the entire container filesystem.

Security considerations

Also protect secrets, avoid host namespace/device mounts, keep images patched/minimal and combine container controls with host/kernel/runtime security.

What I learned

A container is isolated, not magically trusted. Design the privilege inherited after compromise.
